title: The point of no return
subtitle: Wrongful trading, fraudulent trading and disqualification
objectives: State the statutory tests for wrongful trading (s 214/246ZB) and fraudulent trading (s 213) and identify what separates them
Explain the compensatory basis of a wrongful trading declaration and the s 214(3) defence, and connect a finding of unfitness to disqualification under CDDA 1986 s 6
Apply the wrongful trading trigger to a fact pattern and distinguish it from the earlier, equitable Sequana creditor duty

leadingAuthorities.role: Civil wrongful trading — compensation for continuing to trade after insolvent liquidation became unavoidable
Extends the wrongful trading regime to companies that enter administration rather than liquidation
Fraudulent trading — requires actual dishonest intent, unlike wrongful trading

leadingAuthorities.citation: Re Produce Marketing Consortium Ltd (No 2) [1989] 5 BCC 569
leadingAuthorities.role: Fixes the date liability begins and the compensatory (not penal) measure of a s 214 contribution
Mandatory disqualification of directors found unfit following an insolvent liquidation

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This is where directors' duties stop being abstract and start being personal. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can state s 214 — this lesson is about spotting the date it starts to bite on a real set of facts.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans hard on application: expect a set of accounts and a timeline, not a definition to recite.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and don't rush the statutory language in s 214(2) — the whole lesson, including the comparison with Sequana in lesson 8, depends on knowing exactly what triggers the section.

overview.hook: A company can lose money lawfully for years — that's what business risk means, and directors are not insurers of a venture's success. Then, on one particular day, that changes: continuing to trade stops being a bet and starts being a wrong. This lesson is about finding that day, proving what the directors knew about it, and working out what it costs them personally once a liquidator comes looking.

parts.heading: Why 'the company lost money' is not the test
parts.voice: argumentative — states the case for director immunity, then narrows it
body: Limited liability exists precisely so that people will take commercial risks: found a company, borrow to grow it, trade through a bad quarter, and if it fails, the loss falls on the company's creditors and shareholders, not on the director's own house. Ordinary business failure — even reckless overtrading, even bad judgement — is not, on its own, a source of personal liability for a director.

Wrongful trading is the statutory exception that puts a hard stop on that protection. Insolvency Act 1986, s 214 allows a court, on the liquidator's application, to order a director to personally contribute to the company's assets — but only once a specific factual trigger is met. Before that point, trading on is business risk. After it, trading on is wrongful trading, however honestly the director believed things would turn around.

Section 246ZB extends the identical test to companies that go into administration rather than liquidation — a 2015 reform that closed an obvious gap: a director who let a company trade on recklessly shouldn't escape liability just because insolvency practitioners chose one procedure over another.

components.definition: A civil, compensatory wrong under IA 1986 s 214 (liquidation) or s 246ZB (administration): a director who knew, or ought to have concluded, that insolvent liquidation could not reasonably be avoided, and who then failed to take every step to minimise creditor loss, can be ordered to contribute personally to the company's assets.

interaction.prompt: A director keeps trading through a genuinely difficult but not hopeless quarter, making honest commercial judgement calls that later turn out badly. On this alone, is the director exposed to a wrongful trading declaration?
options: No — ordinary business risk and honest misjudgement, without more, are not wrongful trading
Yes — any trading loss exposes a director once the company later becomes insolvent
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Wrongful trading needs the specific s 214(2) trigger — knowledge (actual or constructive) that insolvent liquidation could not reasonably be avoided. Hindsight losses alone never supply that.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not on these facts. Section 214 is not a general penalty for business failure — it bites only once a director knew, or ought to have concluded, that insolvent liquidation was unavoidable. Ordinary bad luck or misjudgement doesn't meet that test.

parts.heading: Reading s 214: the trigger, and the way out
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: Section 214(2) is the provision to know cold, because every wrongful trading problem question is really an argument about whether its conditions are satisfied on a given set of facts. Three things must be true: the company has gone into insolvent liquidation; before the winding up began, the director knew, or ought to have concluded, there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation; and the person was a director at that time.

That middle limb carries a blended test: s 214(4) measures the director against the general knowledge, skill and experience reasonably expected of someone carrying out their functions (an objective floor that applies to everyone, however inexperienced) — but if the actual director has more knowledge, skill or experience than that, they are held to their own higher standard too. A sole director who happens to be a qualified insolvency accountant cannot claim the protection of an ordinary standard.

Section 214(3) then supplies the only defence: even once the trigger is met, a director avoids liability by showing they took every step, from that point on, that they ought to have taken to minimise the potential loss to creditors — which in practice usually means stopping new credit, taking proper professional advice promptly, and documenting the response, not simply hoping the position would improve.

components.text: This subsection applies in relation to a person if the company has gone into insolvent liquidation; at some time before the commencement of the winding up of the company, that person knew or ought to have concluded that there was no reasonable prospect that the company would avoid going into insolvent liquidation; and that person was a director of the company at that time. The court shall not make a declaration under this section with respect to any person if it is satisfied that, after the condition in subsection (2)(b) was first satisfied in relation to that person, they took every step with a view to minimising the potential loss to the company's creditors as they ought to have taken.
elements: Company has gone into insolvent liquidation
Before winding up began: knew or ought to have concluded no reasonable prospect of avoiding it
Person was a director at that time
Defence: every step taken thereafter to minimise creditor loss

interaction.prompt: Under s 214(4), a director with genuinely more financial expertise than an ordinary director in their position is judged against which standard?
options: Their own higher actual knowledge and skill, on top of the objective minimum everyone is held to
Only the objective minimum, regardless of their actual expertise
No standard — expertise is irrelevant to s 214
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Section 214(4) sets an objective floor for everyone, then adds a subjective ceiling: a director cannot rely on an ordinary standard if they in fact knew, or should have known, more.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at the two-limb structure in s 214(4). The objective standard is a floor, not a cap — a director with greater actual knowledge or expertise is held to that higher standard as well.

parts.heading: Finding the date: Re Produce Marketing Consortium
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: Produce Marketing Consortium Ltd imported and distributed fruit. By the mid-1980s its accounts showed a company sliding steadily into insolvency: mounting overdraft, worsening trading losses, accounts that on any competent reading no longer supported the belief that the company could trade its way out. Two directors, Mr Halls and Mr Ward, kept the company trading regardless, drawing on the overdraft to keep suppliers paid, for roughly another eighteen months.

Knox J had to do two distinct jobs. First, fix the date: on the evidence — in particular, the accounts that were, or ought to have been, available to the directors — the point at which no reasonable director in their position could still have concluded the company had a reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation. He found that date well before the company actually stopped trading. Second, work out what the directors owed for the period after that date.

The measure of compensation matters as much as the finding of liability. Knox J held that a s 214 contribution is compensatory, not penal: it is measured by the increase in the net deficiency of the company's assets during the period of wrongful trading — the additional hole the company was dug into by continuing to trade after the trigger date — not the company's total debts, and not a punishment for the original decision to start the business at all.

components.factsShort: Directors of a fruit-importing company kept trading for around 18 months after their own accounts showed insolvent liquidation could no longer reasonably be avoided.
components.ratioShort: A s 214 contribution is compensatory: measured by the increase in the company's net deficiency during the wrongful trading period, from the date the s 214(2) trigger was first met.

expanded.facts: PMC's financial position deteriorated steadily through the mid-1980s. Its own management accounts, reviewed with ordinary competence, disclosed the deterioration well before the directors stopped trading. The company was eventually placed into insolvent liquidation and the liquidator applied under s 214.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Knox J held that the directors ought to have concluded, from a specific identifiable date fixed by reference to the accounts available to them, that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation. From that date, continuing to trade on credit exposed the company's creditors to further loss, and the directors were liable to contribute the amount by which the net deficiency increased between that date and the commencement of winding up.
expanded.significance: This is the leading illustration of how a s 214 claim is actually quantified. It confirms the trigger date is a question of fact tied to what competent directors ought to have read in their own financial information, and that the remedy repairs the specific damage caused by trading on — it does not treat the directors as guarantors of the whole company's debts.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that would most directly help a liquidator identify PMC's wrongful trading trigger date.
interaction.scenarioText: The directors had been running the company for several years. Trading conditions in the fruit import sector were generally difficult across the industry that decade. The company's own management accounts, reviewed at the time, showed a mounting overdraft and worsening losses well before the directors stopped trading. The company eventually entered insolvent liquidation.
tappableSpans: running the company for several years
difficult across the industry that decade
showed a mounting overdraft and worsening losses
interaction.correctSpan: showed a mounting overdraft and worsening losses
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The trigger date in Re Produce Marketing Consortium was fixed by reference to what the company's own accounts disclosed, or ought to have disclosed, to a reasonably competent director — that's the evidence a liquidator builds the claim around, not general industry conditions or how long the directors had served.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Industry-wide difficulty and length of service don't fix a trigger date — every company in a hard sector would otherwise be in the same position. Knox J anchored the date to the company's own financial information and what it disclosed, or ought to have disclosed, to the directors.

parts.heading: Wrongful trading vs fraudulent trading: the dishonesty line
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the tests will probe
body: Section 213 looks like a close cousin of s 214 — both let a liquidator apply for a contribution from those responsible once a company has gone into insolvent liquidation — but the two provisions sit on opposite sides of a hard line. Fraudulent trading under s 213 requires proof that the business was carried on with intent to defraud creditors, or for any other fraudulent purpose. That is a species of actual dishonesty, assessed to the civil standard but requiring genuinely dishonest conduct, not mere carelessness or over-optimism.

Wrongful trading requires none of that. A director who is honestly, even earnestly, convinced the company will pull through — but who ought to have concluded otherwise on the evidence in front of them — is squarely within s 214. That is the whole point of the provision: it exists because dishonesty is hard to prove and honest incompetence causes creditors exactly the same loss.

The practical consequence is that fraudulent trading claims are rare and wrongful trading claims are the liquidator's usual tool. There is also a criminal analogue to fraudulent trading (Companies Act 2006, s 993, requiring the same dishonest intent) with no equivalent criminal offence for wrongful trading at all — another marker of how differently the law treats honest failure and deliberate fraud.

components.text: If in the course of the winding up of a company it appears that any business of the company has been carried on with intent to defraud creditors of the company or creditors of any other person, or for any fraudulent purpose, the court, on the application of the liquidator, may declare that any persons who were knowingly parties to the carrying on of the business in that manner are to be liable to make such contributions (if any) to the company's assets as the court thinks proper.
elements: Business carried on with intent to defraud creditors, or for any fraudulent purpose
Respondent was knowingly a party to that conduct
Contrast with s 214: no dishonest intent required, only the objective/constructive knowledge trigger

interaction.prompt: Which scenario is properly analysed under s 213 (fraudulent trading) rather than s 214 (wrongful trading)?
interaction.scenarioA: A director genuinely believes a delayed contract will rescue the company and keeps trading on credit for three more months after the accounts show no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation.
interaction.scenarioB: A director keeps taking customer deposits for goods they know will never be delivered, using the cash to pay off a personal debt, while telling staff the company is thriving.
interaction.explanation: B shows actual dishonest intent — taking money for goods known never to be supplied, and lying about the company's position — which is fraudulent trading. A is the classic honest-but-wrong wrongful trading fact pattern: no dishonesty, just a failure to recognise, or act on, the point of no return.

parts.heading: Two duties, two triggers: don't conflate this lesson with Sequana
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by drawing the boundary its own material sits inside
body: Lesson 8 taught the *Sequana* creditor duty: directors must have regard to, and eventually act in, the interests of creditors once the company enters something close to insolvency — a modification of the ordinary s 172 duty to promote the success of the company, triggered once directors know, or ought to know, that insolvency is probable. That is an equitable, fiduciary duty. Breach of it is dealt with like any breach of a director's general duty — an account of profits, equitable compensation, and so on.

Wrongful trading is a different creature entirely, and examiners reward students who can hold both apart. It is a freestanding statutory cause of action, not a fiduciary duty. It only arises once the company has actually gone into insolvent liquidation (or administration, under s 246ZB) — Sequana's duty can bite years before any formal insolvency process starts. And its trigger is set at a specific, higher bar: not merely a probability of insolvency, but no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation at all.

Put the two side by side and the relationship becomes clear: Sequana is about how a director must weigh creditors' interests earlier, in the zone of insolvency, while still trying to save the company; s 214 is about what happens if the company doesn't survive and the director kept trading on past the point that outcome became unavoidable. A company can breach neither, either, or both — they are not alternative labels for the same wrong.

components.title: Sequana creditor duty vs s 214 wrongful trading
components.description: A comparison of the two regimes students most often conflate.

nodes.label: Sequana creditor duty (Lesson 8): equitable modification of s 172; triggers once insolvency becomes probable; applies while the company may still be rescued; remedy = breach of duty remedies

Wrongful trading (s 214/246ZB): freestanding statutory cause of action; triggers only once no reasonable prospect remains of avoiding insolvent liquidation; only actionable once the company has actually entered liquidation or administration; remedy = compensatory contribution
Trigger point: 'probability of insolvency' (Sequana) is an earlier and lower bar than 'no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation' (s 214)

components.textAlternative: The Sequana creditor duty and s 214 wrongful trading are frequently conflated but are legally distinct. Sequana is an equitable modification of the s 172 duty, triggered once insolvency becomes probable, and applies while rescue may still be possible; breach is remedied like any breach of directors' duties. Wrongful trading under s 214 (or s 246ZB for administration) is a separate statutory cause of action, only available once the company has actually entered insolvent liquidation or administration, triggered by a later and higher bar — no reasonable prospect of avoiding that outcome — and remedied by a compensatory contribution measured by the increase in net deficiency.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that the Sequana creditor duty and s 214 wrongful trading share the same triggering test?
interaction.explanation: They are different. Sequana's trigger is a probability of insolvency, assessed under an equitable, fiduciary framework, and can apply long before any formal insolvency process. Section 214's trigger is the later, higher threshold of no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation, and only becomes actionable once the company has actually gone into insolvent liquidation or administration.

testPool.prompt: Name the two conditions in IA 1986 s 214(2) that, together with the person being a director, trigger wrongful trading liability.
acceptableAnswers: company gone into insolvent liquidation and director knew or ought to have concluded no reasonable prospect of avoiding it
insolvent liquidation plus knowledge/constructive knowledge of no reasonable prospect of avoiding it
testPool.modelAnswer: The company must have gone into insolvent liquidation, and before winding up began the person must have known, or ought to have concluded, that there was no reasonable prospect the company would avoid insolvent liquidation.

testPool.prompt: Which provision extends the wrongful trading regime to companies that enter administration rather than liquidation?
options: Insolvency Act 1986, s 246ZB
Insolvency Act 1986, s 213

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT required to establish fraudulent trading under s 213?
options: That the business was carried on with intent to defraud creditors, or for a fraudulent purpose
That the respondent was knowingly a party to that conduct
That the company entered insolvent liquidation
That the director personally profited from the fraud
testPool.trapExplanation: Personal profit is not an element of s 213. Liability turns on carrying on the business with intent to defraud, or for any fraudulent purpose, and knowing participation in that — a director can be liable under s 213 even where they did not personally benefit.

testPool.prompt: Put the stages of a s 214 wrongful trading claim in the order a court works through them.
items: The company goes into insolvent liquidation
The court identifies the date the director knew or ought to have concluded there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding it
The court asks whether the director took every step from that date to minimise creditor loss (s 214(3))
If the defence fails, the court quantifies the contribution as the increase in net deficiency from that date

testPool.prompt: Under s 214(4), what is the effect of a director having genuinely less financial skill and experience than would ordinarily be expected of someone in their role?
options: It provides no defence — the objective minimum applies regardless of the director's actual limitations
It automatically excuses the director from any s 214 liability
It shifts the burden of proof to the liquidator to prove dishonesty
testPool.explanation: Section 214(4) sets an objective floor that applies to every director regardless of their actual (lesser) ability — a director cannot plead their own incompetence as a reason to be judged by a lower standard.

testPool.prompt: In this extract adapted from Re Produce Marketing Consortium Ltd (No 2), highlight the sentence that states the measure of a s 214 contribution.
testPool.passage: The directors ought to have concluded, from a date fixed by reference to the company's own accounts, that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation. The contribution payable is not measured by the company's total indebtedness, but by the amount by which the net deficiency of the company's assets increased between that date and the commencement of the winding up. This reflects the compensatory, not penal, purpose of the section.
testPool.ratioSentence: The contribution payable is not measured by the company's total indebtedness, but by the amount by which the net deficiency of the company's assets increased between that date and the commencement of the winding up.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that most clearly signals the wrongful trading trigger has been met.
testPool.scenarioText: The company has had a difficult trading year, with a modest fall in turnover. The finance director's latest management accounts, reviewed at the board, show that liabilities now exceed realisable assets by a wide and widening margin with no credible source of new funding, and that on any competent reading the company cannot pay its debts as they fall due for the foreseeable future. The board continues to place new orders on 60-day credit terms.
tappableSpans: liabilities now exceed realisable assets by a wide and widening margin with no credible source of new funding
continues to place new orders on 60-day credit terms
testPool.correctSpan: liabilities now exceed realisable assets by a wide and widening margin with no credible source of new funding
testPool.explanation: This is the fact that shows no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation — a widening deficiency with no credible funding route, on a competent reading of the accounts. A modest turnover fall alone would not meet the s 214(2) trigger.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is the stronger candidate for the s 214(3) defence succeeding?
testPool.scenarioA: On the trigger date, the director immediately stops taking new orders on credit, takes formal insolvency advice within days, and places the company into administration shortly afterwards.
testPool.scenarioB: On the trigger date, the director continues placing orders on credit for a further four months, hoping a rumoured investor will appear, without seeking professional advice.
testPool.explanation: A shows the director taking every step to minimise creditor loss once the trigger was met — stopping new credit, taking prompt advice, moving to a formal process. B is the textbook wrongful trading fact pattern the defence is designed not to protect.

testPool.prompt: A newly appointed non-executive director joins the board two weeks before the company enters insolvent liquidation, after the wrongful trading trigger date has already passed. Can they be liable under s 214?
options: No — s 214 only applies to a person who was a director at the time the trigger condition was first satisfied
Yes — anyone who was ever a director of an insolvent company is automatically liable
Yes, but only if they personally signed the accounts
testPool.explanation: Section 214(2)(c) requires the person to have been a director at the time the trigger condition was met. A director appointed only after that date is not exposed for the period before their appointment, though their own conduct after joining is separately assessed.

testPool.prompt: A liquidator has established the s 214(2) trigger and wants a director also disqualified. Under CDDA 1986 s 6, what must be shown?
options: That the company became insolvent and the director's conduct makes them unfit to be concerned in the management of a company
That the director was convicted of a criminal offence
That the director personally profited from the wrongful trading
testPool.explanation: Section 6 CDDA 1986 requires insolvency plus a finding of unfitness based on the director's conduct — no criminal conviction or personal profit is required, and a wrongful trading finding is commonly relied on as evidence of unfitness, though the two proceedings are legally distinct.

testPool.prompt: Anya is a director of a retailer. Eight months before liquidation, the company's management accounts show liabilities exceeding assets with no realistic prospect of recovery. Anya reads the accounts, privately worries, but says nothing and continues placing large stock orders on 90-day credit for a further five months, hoping a seasonal sales spike will rescue the company. It does not, and the company enters insolvent liquidation. Analyse Anya's exposure under s 214.
factsToOrder: The accounts, eight months before liquidation, show no realistic prospect of recovery
Anya reads the accounts and privately worries but says nothing
Anya continues placing large stock orders on 90-day credit for five more months
The hoped-for seasonal spike does not materialise

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Anya is liable to contribute to the company's assets for wrongful trading under s 214.
modelAnswer.rule: Section 214(2) requires insolvent liquidation, that the director knew or ought to have concluded there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding it, and that they were a director at that time; s 214(3) provides a defence where every step was taken thereafter to minimise creditor loss; the contribution is measured by the increase in net deficiency from the trigger date (Re Produce Marketing Consortium).
modelAnswer.application: The accounts eight months out show the trigger condition is met on their face, and Anya's own reading of them, followed by continuing to place large orders on credit for a further five months on the strength of hope rather than any credible plan, is the paradigm case the section targets — honest optimism does not satisfy s 214(3), which requires active steps such as stopping new credit or seeking advice. The measure of Anya's contribution would be the increase in the net deficiency caused by trading on for those five months.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Anya is likely liable to contribute under s 214, quantified by the increase in the company's net deficiency during the five months she continued to trade after the trigger date.

testPool.prompt: Why does IA 1986 s 214 not require proof of dishonesty, unlike s 213?
options: Because Parliament intended s 214 to catch honest but negligent or over-optimistic directors, whose conduct causes creditors identical harm to dishonest conduct
Because dishonesty is presumed once a company becomes insolvent
Because s 214 is a criminal offence and dishonesty is assumed from conviction
testPool.trapExplanation: Dishonesty is never presumed from mere insolvency, and s 214 is a civil, not criminal, provision. It deliberately omits a dishonesty requirement because honest but negligent trading-on causes creditors the same loss as dishonest trading-on, and dishonesty is often impossible to prove.

testPool.prompt: Order these events as they would typically unfold from an ordinary struggling company through to a director being disqualified.
items: The company trades through a difficult period with no liability arising
The company passes the s 214(2) trigger point without the directors changing course
The company enters insolvent liquidation and the liquidator investigates
The liquidator obtains a s 214 declaration and separately reports conduct for CDDA s 6 disqualification proceedings

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a director who breaches the Sequana creditor duty has, by that fact alone, also committed wrongful trading under s 214?
testPool.explanation: They are distinct. Sequana's trigger (probability of insolvency) is earlier and lower than s 214's (no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation), and s 214 is only actionable once the company has actually entered insolvent liquidation or administration. A Sequana breach does not automatically establish wrongful trading, and vice versa.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is conflating the Sequana creditor duty (Lesson 8) with statutory wrongful trading. They have different legal bases, different triggers, and different remedies — check which one a question is actually asking about before you start applying either test.
